items.stemHtml: A 26-year-old woman has had 2 days of severe, poorly localised abdominal pain, constipation, vomiting and weakness in both arms. She started an oral contraceptive 3 weeks ago. Temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse 118/min and blood pressure 158/96 mmHg. The abdomen is soft and nontender. Her urine is reddish brown and darkens further after standing in a window. Urine dipstick is negative for blood, and microscopy shows no red blood cells. Serum sodium is 128 mEq/L. Deficiency of which of the following enzymes is most likely?
items.explanationHtml:
Attacks of abdominal pain with a benign abdomen, tachycardia, hypertension, hyponatremia and motor neuropathy, triggered by a drug that induces hepatic ALA synthase, are acute intermittent porphyria. Porphobilinogen deaminase (hydroxymethylbilane synthase) is deficient, so porphobilinogen and aminolevulinic acid accumulate; porphobilinogen oxidises to coloured porphyrins, so urine darkens on standing in light while the heme dipstick stays negative. Treat with hemin and glucose and stop the trigger.

Takeaway: dark urine without heme on dipstick plus neurovisceral attacks after a new drug: think acute intermittent porphyria (porphobilinogen deaminase).

whyNot.A: ALA dehydratase deficiency (or lead inhibition) gives a similar picture but is very rare; lead poisoning would add basophilic stippling and anemia, and porphobilinogen would not be raised.
whyNot.B: Ferrochelatase deficiency causes erythropoietic protoporphyria with painful photosensitivity, not abdominal attacks or dark urine.
whyNot.C: Homogentisate oxidase deficiency (alkaptonuria) darkens urine on standing but causes ochronosis and arthritis, not acute neurovisceral attacks.
whyNot.E: Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase deficiency causes porphyria cutanea tarda: blistering on sun-exposed skin without abdominal attacks.

items.objective: Recognise acute intermittent porphyria as a cause of dark, heme-negative urine with neurovisceral attacks.
